summary: Specifies how to put audio compressed with the ITU-T G.729.1 codec into Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) packets for live streaming over IP. It also registers the media type for the payload format.

eli5.summary: Voices are squeezed into small packages to travel over the internet. This note says exactly how to pack one particular kind of squeezed voice so the other end can unpack it properly.

subtitle: How to carry G.729.1 scalable wideband speech in RTP packets, including an in-band way to ask the other side to slow down.

tldr.problem: G.729.1 is an ITU-T speech codec with 12 embedded bit rates between 8 and 32 kbps, and it needs a standard way to be packed into RTP so that different VoIP products can interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP payload starts with a 1-octet header holding a 4-bit MBS field (the maximum bit rate the sender can receive) and a 4-bit FT field (the frame type), followed by zero or more frames at the same bit rate. A media type, audio/G7291, and its SDP mapping are registered.
tldr.outcome: Senders can change bit rate at any moment without signalling, and receivers can ask for a lower rate in-band. The format has since been updated by RFC 5459.

today: RFC 4749 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 5459.

sections.title: The G.729.1 Codec
sections.content:
G.729.1 is an 8-32 kbps scalable wideband (50-7000 Hz) speech and audio coding algorithm. It is interoperable with G.729, G.729 Annex A and G.729 Annex B, so it offers a smooth transition from narrowband to wideband telephony. The RFC lists IP telephony and videoconferencing as the main services, for enterprise networks or for mass-market uses such as PSTN emulation over DSL or wireless access.

The coder produces an embedded bitstream of 12 layers, one for each of 12 bit rates between 8 and 32 kbps. The first layer, at 8 kbps, is the core layer and is bitstream compatible with G.729/G.729A. A second layer at 12 kbps improves narrowband quality, and upper layers give wideband audio between 14 and 32 kbps in 2 kbps steps. Only the core layer is needed to decode understandable speech.

The codec works on 20-ms frames with a default sampling rate of 16 kHz. Input and output at 8 kHz are also supported at all bit rates.
sections.eli5: Think of a layer cake. The bottom layer is enough to hear what someone says. Each extra layer on top makes the sound clearer and richer.

sections.title: Embedded Bit Rates and the MBS Request
sections.content:
Because the stream is embedded, a sender can change its bit rate at any time without external signalling, and the receiver can still decode the frames. That can help control congestion, or share a fixed-bandwidth voice link between a changing number of calls, for example in a residential or trunking gateway.

Changing the sending rate only affects the sending direction. To adjust the receiving bandwidth too, the RFC introduces an in-band request called MBS (Maximum Bit rate Supported), which asks the other party to change its own sending bit rate.

MBS only helps for two-way unicast G.729.1 traffic. An MBS sent from A to B concerns the stream from B to A, so if there is no G.729.1 stream in the reverse direction it has no effect.
sections.eli5: Two friends are talking over a walkie-talkie. Either one can say "please talk a bit shorter, my line is busy". MBS is that polite request, hidden inside the voice packets.

sections.title: RTP Header Usage
sections.content:
The RTP header follows RFC 3550. The RTP timestamp clock is 16 kHz, the same as the default sampling rate. Even when the encoder input or decoder output runs at 8 kHz, a 16 kHz RTP clock rate MUST always be used, since this does not change the bitstream.

One frame lasts 20 ms, which is 320 samples at 16 kHz, so the timestamp grows by 320 for each consecutive frame. The M bit MUST be set to zero in all packets. The RTP payload type number is not assigned here; the RTP profile in use is expected to assign one or to bind it dynamically.
sections.eli5: The packets carry a clock that ticks the same way every time. Each 20 ms slice of sound moves the clock forward by the same fixed step.

sections.title: The Payload Format
sections.content:
A payload is a 1-octet header followed by zero or more consecutive audio frames, all at the same bit rate. The header has two 4-bit fields.

MBS tells the receiver of this payload the maximum bit rate the sender can accept. The encoder MUST NOT exceed the rate in the MBS it receives, but may send at that rate or any lower one and may change rate at any time. A new MBS overrides the previous one. Values 12 to 14 are reserved and MUST be ignored; value 15 means NO_MBS. It MUST be 15 for packets sent to a multicast group (and ignored when received from one), and in all packets when the MBS is sent by non-RTP means.

FT gives the frame type and so the bit rate and frame size of the frames in the packet, from 0 (8 kbps, 20 octets) to 11 (32 kbps, 80 octets). FT 15 (NO_DATA) means there is no audio, which can be used to update the MBS when there is nothing to send. A payload with a reserved FT value (12 to 14) MUST be ignored entirely.

Frames are packed oldest first. The number of frames is the audio data size divided by the frame size; any remainder bytes are ignored.
sections.eli5: Every package has a tiny label on the front with two numbers: how good the sound inside is, and the best quality the sender wants back. Inside are one or more slices of sound, oldest first.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Negotiation
sections.content:
The RFC registers media type audio/G7291 with optional parameters maxbitrate, mbs, ptime and maxptime. maxbitrate is the absolute maximum codec bit rate for the session (32000 if omitted). mbs is the current maximum bit rate supported as a receiver; it defaults to maxbitrate, must not exceed it, and can be updated dynamically by the MBS field in packets.

In SDP, the subtype goes in a=rtpmap with a clock rate that MUST be 16000, and ptime and maxptime go in their own attributes. The rest go in a=fmtp.

In offer-answer, the offerer SHOULD also list G.729, preferring G.729.1, so G.729-only parties can still talk. maxbitrate is bidirectional and the answer MUST be equal or smaller. mbs is not symmetric, and neither side may start sending above the other's mbs. A value between the limits but not in the permitted set is read as the closest lower valid value; out-of-range values cause rejection. For multicast and declarative SDP (such as SAP and RTSP), mbs MUST NOT be used and maxbitrate is declarative.
sections.eli5: Before a call, both sides agree on the best quality they can both handle and on which older, simpler format to fall back to if one of them is not modern enough.

sections.title: Congestion Control and Security
sections.content:
Congestion control for RTP SHALL follow RFC 3550 and the relevant profile such as RFC 3551. G.729.1's embedded, variable bit rates can help. Packing more frames in each payload reduces header overhead but increases delay and reduces error robustness.

The payload format has no built-in security mechanisms. Confidentiality, integrity and authentication of the audio come from external mechanisms, and SRTP is named as one that MAY be used. The RFC finds no significant non-uniformity in receiver computational load, so pathological datagrams are unlikely to be a denial-of-service threat.
sections.eli5: If the road is crowded, send smaller packages. The packages are not locked by themselves, so use an outside lock if the call is private.

fields.name: MBS
fields.desc: Maximum bit rate the sender of this packet can receive; 15 is NO_MBS.

fields.name: FT
fields.desc: Frame type: bit rate and frame size of the frames that follow; 15 is NO_DATA.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: A payload with these values is ignored.

items.label: NO_DATA
items.desc: No audio in the payload; can carry an MBS update.
